items.title: OML 42: Delta community threatens to shutdown oil operations over spill
items.description: By Jimitota Onoyume Odidi, a host community of OML, 42, in Warri South-West Local Government Area of Delta, has protested over the oil spill in the area, urging the firm and other relevant agencies to quickly come to fix the problem. They alleged that aquatic lives and their environment were being destroyed by the fast spreading crude oil spill, adding that they were even afraid of a likely fire explosion from the incident . “We have lost fishes in our waters and plants in our farms. The crude oil spill has covered our water and even spread to our roads. This can ignite a fire “, one of them said The community, which hosts oil operations within the OML 42 area, stormed the company’s operational facility on Friday, in a peaceful protest. The protesters led by the Secretary of the community , Mr. Clement Numa, and the Public Relations Officer, Comrade Konkemele Michael decried the alleged delay by the firm to fix the oil spill. The protesters warned that unless the company urgently stopped the continuing discharge of crude oil and took immediate steps to contain the spill, they would be forced to shut down oil operations in the area The community alleged that the spill, which they traced to an aged and corroded section of the Trans-Forcados Pipeline around the crude oil loading point at the Keremor manifold, has persisted for about six months, with large volumes of crude allegedly continuing to enter the surrounding waterways. According to the protesters, the pollution has devastated fishing grounds and other traditional sources of livelihood, while residents are increasingly exposed to health and safety risks. They also expressed concern that the continued presence of crude oil in the waterways could trigger a major fire outbreak, potentially resulting in catastrophic loss of lives and property. Addressing journalists during the protest, the community’s PRO, Comrade Konkemele Michael, described the action as a warning to the Federal Government, the National Assembly and relevant regulatory agencies to intervene before the situation escalates. “This is a warning visit and a peaceful protest for us to send the message across to His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, the National Assembly and all regulatory bodies that we will commence drastic action if they do not stop further operations until they curtail the spill,” Michael said. He alleged that the pollution had taken over the community’s waterways and displaced some residents, while others had reportedly been hospitalised. “The oil pollution has taken over the entire community for the past six months and the entire river has been taken over,” he said. Michael further described the incident as one of the most serious oil spills witnessed in the Niger Delta in recent years, accusing the company of continuing its normal operations despite the alleged environmental emergency. He alleged that crude oil was still flowing from the affected point, raising fears of a possible fire outbreak. The community leader also accused the oil firm operating in the area of allegedly attempting to address the crisis through selective distribution of relief materials rather than tackling the alleged source of the pollution. He claimed that some residents had started leaving the community because of fears over the possibility of fire, while alleging that a local contractor engaged by the company had been using a wooden boat without making meaningful progress in containing the spill. The Secretary of the Odidi Community, Mr. Numa, said the community was becoming increasingly frustrated by what he described as the failure to adequately contain the spill. Numa questioned why oil production activities should continue while crude was allegedly still escaping into the environment. “You cannot continue working when oil is still gushing out. The spill should be curtailed immediately,” he said. According to him, oil spills are expected to be reported to the National Oil Spills Detection and Response Agency (NOSDRA) within the prescribed regulatory timeframe, while failure to comply attracts sanctions. Numa argued that the community needed more than relief materials, insisting that the priority should be to stop the source of the pollution, recover the affected environment and protect residents. He further accused the firm of allegedly exploiting divisions within the community by dealing selectively with individuals and groups. The community secretary alleged that selected persons had received food items, including rice and vegetable oil, as well as undisclosed sums of money, which he claimed was being used to deflect attention from the environmental crisis. “The company is trying to avoid the environmental crime being committed against Odidi people,” Numa alleged. Residents and community leaders said the prolonged pollution had severely affected fishing activities, which remain a major source of income and food for households in the riverine community. They called on the Federal Government, NOSDRA, the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) and the Delta State Government to urgently undertake a comprehensive investigation and remediation exercise. The community also demanded medical intervention for residents allegedly exposed to the pollution, environmental impact assessment, restoration of contaminated waterways and transparent monitoring of the cleanup process. The protesters maintained that their action was peaceful but warned that continued inaction could lead to a complete shutdown of oil operations in the area. items.title: Tunisie | Les autorités ne communiquent pas le nombre de morts liées à la canicule
items.description: L’Organisation tunisienne des jeunes médecins (OTJM) a appelé le gouvernement à déclarer l’état d’urgence sanitaire, mettant en garde contre la pression croissante sur les services d’urgence des hôpitaux publics en raison de la hausse des températures. Dans un communiqué publié samedi 28 août 2026, l’organisation a indiqué que les services d’urgence connaissent, selon ses estimations, une augmentation qualifiée d’ «inédite» du nombre d’hospitalisations et de décès liés aux coups de chaleur et aux températures élevées. Elle a également fait état de décès survenus parmi des détenus au sein de plusieurs services d’urgence, coïncidant avec ce qu’elle a décrit comme un état d’ «épuisement extrême» du personnel médical et infirmier, sous l’effet d’une pression dépassant, selon elle, les capacités du système de santé. L’organisation a indiqué que les services compétents du ministère de la Santé avaient, selon ses informations, recensé les données relatives aux décès et aux cas d’insolation, ainsi que celles concernant la capacité d’accueil des services de réanimation, tout en précisant que ces chiffres n’avaient pas encore été officiellement publiés. L’OTJM a réclamé la déclaration immédiate de l’état d’urgence sanitaire, appelant à soutenir les professionnels de santé et à prendre les mesures nécessaires pour faire face aux répercussions de la vague de chaleur et en limiter les risques pour les citoyens. Le ministère de la Santé, pour sa part, préfère ne pas communiquer sur cette question ni donner des statistiques sur le nombre des décès dans les hôpitaux publics, comme si c’était un secret d’Etat. Une position inexplicable et qu’on ne saurait justifier, au moment où, dans les hôpitaux publics, les gens pleurent leurs morts dont les annonces de décès se multiplient sur les réseaux sociaux. Le directeur régional de la santé de Sfax, le Dr Hatem Cherif, reconnaît, néanmoins, que le service des urgences du CHU Habib Bourguiba connaît une forte pression, particulièrement en cette période marquée par une augmentation des cas d’insolation et par l’afflux de nombreux patients venus des gouvernorats voisins pour se faire soigner. Intervenant dans Diwan FM , le Dr Cherif a expliqué que cette pression s’explique par le fait que l’hôpital dispose d’un service d’urgences de niveau 3 couvrant l’ensemble de la région, tout en soulignant l’engagement des équipes médicales à prodiguer des soins à tous les patients, quelle que soit leur zone de résidence. Il s’est cependant gardé d’avancer les chiffres de décès enregistrés par cet établissement en lien avec la canicule de ces derniers jours. C’est à croire que les responsables du secteur ont reçu des instructions strictes à ce propos. I. B. items.title: Axe Kissidougou-Kankan : « nous sommes fatigués », les chauffeurs dénoncent la dégradation de la route
items.description: Entre Kissidougou et Kankan, la saison des pluies complique fortement les déplacements. Sur le tronçon compris entre Moribaya et Tokounou, la boue, les nids-de-poule et la dégradation de la chaussée ralentissent la circulation. Chauffeurs, passagers et transporteurs décrivent des voyages qui s’allongent, des véhicules immobilisés et des pannes à répétition. Certains voyageurs affirment même passer des nuits sur la route. Entre Moribaya et Tokounou, une chaussée difficile Sur cet axe qui relie la Guinée forestière à la Haute-Guinée, certains passages deviennent particulièrement difficiles à franchir pendant l’hivernage. La boue s’accumule sur plusieurs portions. Les trous rendent également la progression des véhicules plus compliquée, notamment pour les camions et les véhicules de transport. Pour les chauffeurs, ces difficultés rallongent considérablement la durée des trajets. Mamoudou Cissé, chauffeur qui emprunte régulièrement cet axe, raconte les difficultés rencontrées lors de son dernier voyage : « Vous voyez la boue, elle nous a vraiment fatigués. Depuis avant-hier à 17 heures, nous avons quitté Guéckédou et jusqu’à présent, nous sommes toujours sur la route. Nous ne sommes pas encore rentrés. Cela fait deux ans que je suis sur cette route. La route n’est pas bonne. Quand la saison des pluies arrive, notre bonheur est fini. Il y a des trous et la boue est trop importante. » Depuis deux ans, Mamoudou Cissé transporte notamment des produits agricoles comme la banane, l’aubergine et le piment. Selon lui, les difficultés sont particulièrement importantes pendant la saison des pluies. Des véhicules exposés aux pannes L’état de la chaussée entraîne également des conséquences sur les véhicules. Pneus endommagés, pièces mécaniques défectueuses et immobilisations prolongées figurent parmi les difficultés évoquées par les chauffeurs. Ces dépenses viennent s’ajouter aux coûts habituels liés au transport et à l’entretien des véhicules. Mamoudou Cissé explique pourquoi, malgré ces difficultés, il continue d’emprunter cet axe : « C’est ici que nous cherchons notre nourriture. Si j’avais les moyens, je n’allais pas pratiquer cette route pendant cette période d’hivernage. Nos pneus sont gâtés, on les change. » Des pannes qui prolongent les voyages Sur le terrain, les conséquences sont visibles. Des véhicules restent immobilisés dans la boue pendant plusieurs heures. Abdoulaye Kourouma, chauffeur sur le tronçon Guéckédou–Mandiana, dit avoir été confronté à une panne qui a retardé son déplacement. Il revient sur les heures d’attente nécessaires pour remettre son véhicule en circulation : « Nous sommes fatigués. Notre disque est grillé. Nous avons changé entre 3 heures et 5 heures avant de pouvoir bouger. Et devant nous, nous avons trouvé que la route n’était toujours pas bonne. Ils disent qu’ils ont fait la route. Mais quand tu fais un voyage, au deuxième voyage, tu retrouves la route dans un mauvais état. Je ne sais pas s’ils ne veulent pas faire notre route ou pas. » Pour les chauffeurs, les difficultés ne concernent donc pas uniquement la durée du trajet. Elles touchent également les conditions de travail des conducteurs et de leurs apprentis ainsi que le confort des passagers. Lancinet Cissé, autre chauffeur présent sur l’axe, décrit une situation similaire. Depuis la route, il évoque les conséquences de ces conditions sur les voyageurs et les véhicules : « Je suis vraiment fatigué par l’état de la route. La route n’est pas bonne. S’ils peuvent faire cette route entre Kankan et Tokounou, c’est du calvaire. Quand nous apprêtons, c’est de la fatigue. Nos véhicules tombent en panne, les passagers se fatiguent, les chauffeurs et les apprentis aussi. Depuis qu’on est sortis hier jusqu’à présent, nous ne sommes pas encore arrivés à Kankan. » Des voyageurs passent des jours sur la route Les difficultés concernent également les passagers qui empruntent cet itinéraire. Les longs temps de parcours peuvent transformer un déplacement de quelques heures en voyage de plusieurs jours. Peter Samuel, un passager en provenance de Sierra Leone, affirme avoir passé deux jours sur la route. Il décrit son expérience et appelle à une attention accrue sur l’état de cet axe : « Nous avons fait deux jours sur la route. L’état de la route est terrible. Traverser cette route relève d’un parcours de combattant. Nous avons beaucoup souffert. Ce ne sera pas la dernière fois que je viendrai. Je reviendrai encore à Siguiri pour rendre visite à ma sœur. Mais la maintenance des routes doit être une priorité pour les autorités. » Au-delà des difficultés vécues par les voyageurs, l’état de la route peut également affecter l’acheminement des produits agricoles vers les différents marchés du pays. Pour les transporteurs, les retards et les pannes peuvent entraîner des coûts supplémentaires et compliquer la livraison des marchandises. Les usagers demandent des travaux Sur cet axe reliant la Guinée forestière à la Haute-Guinée, les témoignages recueillis font état de difficultés récurrentes pendant la saison des pluies : boue, nids-de-poule, pannes mécaniques, pneus endommagés et longues heures d’attente. Les usagers demandent donc aux autorités de renforcer les travaux d’entretien et de réhabilitation afin d’améliorer les conditions de circulation. En attendant d’éventuels travaux, chauffeurs, passagers et transporteurs continuent de composer avec une route dont l’état complique davantage les déplacements pendant l’hivernage. Reportage de Karifa Kansan depuis Tokounou. items.title: Social media is now your public reference point – Joyce Bawah Mogtari
items.description: Senior Presidential Aide and Advisor to President John Dramani Mahama, Joyce Bawah Mogtari, has urged social media users to be deliberate about what they publish online, stressing that social media profiles have increasingly become public reference points. She said the growing influence of social media makes it an important tool for communication, business, political campaigns, public engagement and marketing, and encouraged users to leverage the platforms to promote constructive ideas and meaningful conversations. “Social media advocacy and advertising have become powerful tools and essential skills for modern-day communication, business, political campaigns, public engagement, and marketing. Apparently, your social media handles are now your public reference point. So be careful what you post or comment on,” she said. In a Facebook post, Madam Mogtari explained that her personal platforms serve largely as an extension of her work as a spokesperson and communicator, as well as a channel for amplifying the work of the NDC. She said disagreements and personal differences should not prevent people from using social media positively. She encouraged users to consistently share thoughtful, well-researched and relevant content, arguing that such an approach could attract engagement from people outside their immediate networks, including professionals and individuals they may never have met. “Social media is ultimately about networking, exchanging ideas, building relationships, and creating connections. The key is to use your platform wisely to contribute to social change, promote meaningful ideas, and participate in constructive conversations,” she added.

items.title: Pick Up Where You Left Off
items.description: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight. Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning. Think about something that you loved doing when you were younger. Maybe you drew, played an instrument, wrote stories, or spent hours learning about something just because it fascinated you. Then school got busier, work took over, or the hobby started to feel less useful than everything else that was competing for your time. In 2023, David Brooks wrote an Atlantic article about people entering a new stage of life after their primary career. Many realized that, on the way up the professional ladder, they had abandoned interests and ambitions that had once mattered to them. In their 60s, they began picking up those lost strands. “The human hunger for meaning and fulfillment is strong,” Brooks wrote. “We shouldn’t have to wait until we’re 65 to learn how to transform our lives.” Returning to an old interest can remind you what it feels like to do something without needing it to lead anywhere. The point is not to re-create your childhood but to make room for interests that don’t fit neatly into the life you’ve already built. This weekend, return to something that you had quietly stopped doing. Pick up the book, racket, paintbrush, or instrument. You may find that you’ve indeed outgrown it—or wonder why you ever put it down. On Returning to What You Love The New Old Age By David Brooks What a new life stage can teach the rest of us about how to find meaning and purpose—before it’s too late ( From 2023 ) Read the article. How to Be Happy Growing Older By Arthur C. Brooks Your future will probably be better than your past. ( From 2023 ) Read the article. The Curious Personality Changes of Older Age By Faith Hill When people lose the ability to control their circumstances, their selves sometimes evolve instead. ( From 2023 ) Read the article. Still Curious? What I wish I’d known when I was younger : Last year, Arthur C. Brooks argued that the three reasons old people are happier can work for any age. Semi-retirees know the key to work-life balance : More and more older adults are working—in large part because they want to, Kate Cray wrote in 2023. Other Diversions Watching Tim Curry have fun was the most fun thing. What a bicentennial baby knows A turning point in AI writing PS Courtesy of Dennis L. My colleague Isabel Fattal recently asked readers to share a photo of something that sparks their sense of awe in the world. “The bristlecone; awe on a multi-millennial scale,” Dennis L. writes. We’ll continue to feature your responses in the coming weeks. Reply to this email with a photo and a short description. — Rafaela

items.title: The Real Appeal of the Internet’s Favorite Terrible Movie
items.description: One of the only compliments I can offer the new Chinese animated film Niu Lai is that it certainly qualifies as a film. There is sound. The pictures move. But beyond the basics of what makes a movie a movie, Niu Lai , which translates to “The Ox Comes,” contains little artistic merit. The plot, about a calf coming of age with the help of a leopard, a bird, and his mother, is thin, and the characters have been so nightmarishly rendered on a rudimentary computer program that they might as well be sleep-paralysis demons. Yet Niu Lai has become a bona fide box-office hit in China. Since a small distributor unceremoniously dumped it in theaters in early August, the film has become one of the most lucrative movies in Chinese history, making more than $7 million off a reported budget of no more than $500 and outperforming recent blockbusters such as The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day . Much of its success is thanks to Chinese social media, where clips of it first went viral: Some users have embraced Niu Lai as a meme, purchasing tickets so they could ridicule the baffling work with an audience. Others have championed the project as anti-AI art, arguing that it deserves to be appreciated as a purely human creation. As flawed as Niu Lai may be, to the fans, it’s at least better than AI slop. I’m not so sure about that. Watching a bootleg version of Niu Lai felt painful but apt: What better way was there to see a jankily made film than in potato quality on my computer at home? Instead, what’s distinctly human about Niu Lai comes from everything around it: how it was made, how it became a sensation, and how it has inspired further creativity in turn. Theater workers have drawn posters by hand to help advertise the movie. Businesses have made plush toys of the bovine hero. Fans have donned cow masks for screenings, and although the film isn’t available in the United States, underground viewings have popped up in major cities. As such, Niu Lai is the rare passion project that has attracted audiences not because it’s so bad that it’s good, but because it’s an occasion to celebrate the ability to have an original idea at all. [ Read: Why a Chinese animated film has made more money than any Star Wars sequel ] Never mind that the idea was apparently underdeveloped from the start. The first-time director, Xin Yumeng, explained in an interview that he wanted to write about an ox because that’s his father’s zodiac symbol; the year he began working on it also happened to be 2021, the year of the ox. Production took five years, as the then-29-year-old Xin and his mother, Sun Lifang, wrote the screenplay together and made up the entire crew and cast: Sun sang the theme song, and Xin animated the 86-minute film frame by frame on SketchUp, an architectural-modeling program. The process was grueling, Xin said, adding that he kept going in part because he saw the story as a way to inspire viewers to not tang ping , or “lie flat,” referring to a societal trend in 2021 where young people in China rejected overworking by cheekily glorifying the act of lying down. In some ways, the movie is a deeply Chinese phenomenon: Fuzzy cartoon characters tend to become popular in the country— Zootopia 2 is the highest-grossing Hollywood film ever released there—and the words niu lai could also refer to the coming of a bull market, which has led some Chinese stock investors to purchase tickets for good luck. Plus, Niu Lai ’s threadbare plot is rooted in the principle of filial piety, as the titular protagonist learns to respect and care for his mother. The Niu Lai phenomenon also seems to embody a phrase that’s gained traction lately in China: huo ren gan , which, translated literally, means “alive-human feeling.” The film expresses this quality, but not only because Xi didn’t use AI to help create it. What makes Niu Lai stand out most is its unabashed sincerity. It is an earnest attempt to tell a fable about a naive cow, and the story of its making is deeply charming: Here is a mother-son duo, total outsiders to the entertainment industry, trying their best to turn their quixotic idea into reality. Making a movie anywhere requires overcoming so many hurdles that have nothing to do with art or creativity; there are budgets to be balanced and business expectations to be met. But Niu Lai is a modest reminder that any film simply begins with an idea and an irrepressible urge to see it through.

items.title: A New Way of Seeing Alien Worlds
items.description: Tomorrow morning, if all goes to plan, NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, its latest and greatest orbital observatory, will lift off from its launchpad and add a little rocket-booster light to the Florida sunshine. A lot is riding on this mission. If the Roman is successful, it could give humanity a new way to see the planets around other stars and a fresh understanding of the largest-scale objects that we know to exist. But if it fails, NASA’s science program, which is already fending off ruinous budget cuts , will need to seriously rethink its future. The Artemis mission to the moon was a big win for human spaceflight, and now the science side of the house badly needs one. NASA’s engineers have spent more than a decade readying the Roman for this moment. Before the telescope arrived in Florida, it spent more than a year in NASA’s largest clean room at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland. To get near it, you had to be mummified alive. When I visited in December, NASA staffers led me to a sterile, fluorescent-lit locker room. They tossed me a white jumpsuit and two sets of booties with tight-fitting straps. They told me to put on a beard net and hair net, and triple-wrapped the gap between my jumpsuit sleeves and gloves with blue tape. The astronomers didn’t want my skin exposed in the clean room. Dry flakes of it could drift off and settle onto the telescope’s ultrasmooth primary mirror. “You’re going to be the dirtiest thing in here,” one of them told me, as we walked through a little chamber where more than 30 nozzles blasted us with air. I jotted down this remark on special mint-green paper that sheds fewer particulates than a regular notebook, and then stepped into a cavernous eight-story white space soundtracked by the hum of six school-bus-size fans. At its center, the Roman stood more than 40 feet high, and it was surrounded by more than a dozen people, all in identical jumpsuits. Half were standing in clusters, talking, while the other half were up on motorized lifts, fussing with the telescope, applying duct tape and making final adjustments. More than a thousand people have worked on this project, and those who are lucky enough to get close to the hardware seem to derive a physical pleasure from the experience. [ Read: Inside Donald Trump’s attack on NASA’s science missions ] The Roman has a pretty shady backstory for a scientific instrument. Its primary mirror was part of a surprise gift bestowed on NASA by the National Reconnaissance Office. The NRO is one of America’s most secretive government agencies, and it apparently had a Hubble-class spare just lying around. A cash-strapped agency can’t afford to be too choosy about provenance: NASA took this mirror that was supposed to point down at the ground , for surveillance, and will instead point it out at the stars. Coronagraph delivery and unboxing (Chris Gunn / NASA) The NRO’s spare mirror has also solved a bit of internal politics for NASA’s science program. The Roman is built to monitor the universe at the very largest scales, to map the cosmic superstructure of galaxy clusters that stretches out from us in every direction, to see how it has expanded over time. These observations might lead scientists to a more refined sense for gravity, and may even help them discover new physics. But the idea for a mission like this was originally conceived of around the early 2000s, shortly after the discovery of dark energy , and a survey of the large-scale universe seemed like the obvious next thing to do. When NASA was finally ready to build the telescope, in the early 2010s, the action in astronomy had shifted closer to home. Scientists were in the midst of discovering thousands of new planets around nearby stars, and they wanted to find more. Although the Roman’s original mission plan did allow for some planet-hunting, the new mirror would allow them to do it in a whole new way. [ Read: The Nobel Prize winner who thinks we have the universe all wrong ] Finding a little world with its own atmosphere in the glare of a nearby star is tricky work. Even the very largest planets will be a billion times fainter than the suns they orbit. When I spoke with Dominic Benford, Roman’s program scientist at NASA Headquarters, he likened the challenge to spotting a firefly buzzing around a powerful searchlight from thousands of miles away. To make this possible, astronomers have lodged an exquisite new kind of coronagraph into the Roman’s metallic guts. Coronagraphs originally helped astronomers see the plasma flares emanating from our sun, by blocking out the far more brilliant light from the solar disk. In a sense, the device creates a brief artificial eclipse inside the telescope. The Roman’s coronagraph is designed to do something similar for more distant stars so that astronomers can see the planets that surround them. When the telescope is trained on a star in our Milky Way, it will catch a lot of light, and then run it through the coronagraph’s system of barriers and mirrors. Two of the mirrors that it uses may be even more beautiful in their design than the ultrasmooth, eight-foot primary. Each is smaller than the average makeup compact, and has more than 1,600 actuators that can individually deform tiny portions of the glass in tiny increments, less than the diameter of a helium atom. Astronomers will employ hundreds of these warping movements, spread across the mirrors, to deflect a specific star’s glare, creating an image of the star within a ring of nearly pure darkness. Deformable mirrors like these have previously been used on the ground to help telescopes see through the warble and blur of Earth’s atmosphere. But no one has ever sent one of this complexity to space. The Roman team believes that up there, where the viewing conditions are more pristine, the Roman will be able to deliver the first direct images of distant planets in visible light. Until now, most of the extrasolar planets that scientists have observed have been detected indirectly. In some cases, a planet’s existence is inferred from the gravitational force that it exerts on its host star, causing the star to wobble. Or astronomers might see a host star dim, repeatedly and predictably, as an orbiting planet passes in front of it. We have been able to get direct snapshots of only a few young planets that were still roiling hot and glowing brightly, and mainly in infrared. The Roman telescope’s coronagraph should be able to see worlds that aren’t glowing at all. Like Earth, they will be illuminated solely by the soft visible light of their host stars. [ Read: When a telescope is a national-security risk ] I asked Vanessa Bailey, the coronagraph’s instrument technologist, if there were any particular stars that she was excited to inspect. Because the coronagraph isn’t part of the telescope’s main mission, just three of the first 18 months will be set aside for its observations. Bailey said that the astronomers will use that time to look at previously detected planets that are only tens of light-years away. She mentioned the Epsilon Eridani system, where a Jupiter-size world is known to orbit an orange dwarf star. With the coronagraph, they’ll stare at it for many hours, letting photons from the planet slowly pile up. “It’s just going to be a little fuzzy smudge, just barely there,” Bailey said. “But we might be able to tell if it’s cloudy or clear, and we might be able to say whether it’s more like Jupiter or Neptune.” All of this could go wrong. Bailey told me that the coronagraph has never been tested outside the lab, and in space, it may not work. If for some reason the mirrors are misaligned, or the instrument malfunctions, any planets would be lost in the astral glare. NASA’s long-running quest to find another living world in the universe would be set back, perhaps by a decade or more. But if the coronagraph does fulfill its mission, it will serve as a proof of concept for NASA’s next really big telescope, the Habitable Worlds Observatory, which the agency has been developing for more than a decade. Roman’s coronagraph will be able to find only large planets—Saturn-size or ideally bigger—that circle their stars in chilly, distant orbits. NASA scientists want to place a much more precise one on the HWO. That mission will fixate on more than 100 nearby stars that share the sun’s rough age and brightness. Its coronagraph will cast a much tighter ring of near darkness around them, to see if any planets show up in the closer, warmer orbits that might be more hospitable to life—and it will even look for signs of life in the planets’ atmospheres. But the HWO won’t lift off until the late 2030s at the earliest. For now, the Roman has to prove out. It has to survive the violence of launch and fly a million miles from Earth so that its mirrors can catch the light of a nearby star and then surround it in darkness so deep that a faint alien world appears.

items.title: Nigeria will not miss World Cup for 8yrs if I become president — Sowore
items.description: The Presidential candidate of the African Action Congress (AAC) in the 2027 general elections, Mr Omoyele Sowore, has promised to make Nigeria a major global sports hub if elected president. Sowore stated this on Saturday in Enugu while participating in the 2026 Enugu City International Marathon. He said under his administration, Nigeria would not miss any FIFA World Cup during his eight-year tenure, while also developing other sporting disciplines to compete successfully at the international level. The AAC presidential candidate, who participated in the 10-kilometre race for the second time, said he returned to the event after being impressed by the organisation of the previous edition. “Well, I came back because I was impressed with the first one and I have seen so far that the organisation is impressive,” he said. Sowore described road races as important for promoting healthy living, community development and youth engagement, urging every state in Nigeria to organise road races. He, however, clarified that a 10-kilometre race was not technically a marathon, noting that a full marathon was 42 kilometres while a half marathon was 21 kilometres. According to him, sporting events improve health, build communities and create an intersection between sports and culture. He said sports could also help Nigeria develop young people into global ambassadors while creating a significant economic opportunity for the country. “Most importantly, this is how to build young people to be global ambassadors of your country. There’s a big economy out there that is known as the sports economy. “We call it the orange economy. It’s an economic model that, if well-developed, can bring more money than oil,” he said. Sowore cited Brazil and Kenya as examples of countries benefiting significantly from sports, particularly football and long-distance running. “Nigeria has 200 million people. I don’t know why we are not beating Kenya in all the long-distance races,” he said. He promised that, if elected, his administration would develop sports infrastructure and provide an enabling environment for athletes to excel in various sporting disciplines. “Nigeria will become a major sports hub for the world. It doesn’t matter which sports you are doing. I’m a swimmer too, by the way. “I come from the Niger Delta region. I don’t know why we are not winning swimming medals. We have great runners,” he said. Sowore also criticised the country’s sports administration, particularly the management of football, saying Nigeria had the talent to perform better internationally. He said the country had missed opportunities to develop its sporting potential because of poor administration and inadequate support for athletes. He said Nigeria’s failure to qualify for the World Cup was unacceptable, stressing that his administration would ensure that the country consistently qualified for the tournaments. “We are supposed to be at the World Cup. If I’m president of Nigeria, we are not missing any World Cup for my eight years. I’ll make sure that happens. “This is because we get the best and the most competent and we will provide the environment for sports to thrive in this country,” he said. The post Nigeria will not miss World Cup for 8yrs if I become president — Sowore appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Nigeria’s borders not closed, Tunji-Ojo tells Atiku
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi Minister of Interior, Hon. Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, has dismissed claims by former Vice President Atiku Abubakar that Nigeria’s land borders remain closed, insisting there is nothing left to reopen since the borders were not shut in the first place. In a statement reacting to comments credited to Atiku on his plan to reopen Nigeria’s land borders if elected President in 2027, Tunji-Ojo, who supervises the Nigeria Immigration Service NIS as the agency of government in charge of border control and migration management, said it was expedient to correct the record. “As the Minister of Interior who supervises the Nigeria Immigration Service being an agency of government in charge of border control and migration management, it is expedient to state that Nigerian borders are not closed and so cannot be reopened,” he said in a statement issued Saturday in Abuja. The minister traced the sequence of border reopenings over the past several years, noting that the previous government had reopened Seme, Illela, Maigatari and Mfum on 16th December 2020, with others following afterwards. He said Idiroko and Ikom were reopened for goods and services on 20th April 2022, while Kamba and Tsamiya in Kebbi State, linking to Niger Republic and Benin Republic respectively, were reopened under the current administration in February 2026. Tunji-Ojo specifically faulted Atiku’s reference to Cameroon, Chad, Niger and Benin Republic, arguing that the prolonged closures on the Cameroon border at Banki and Amchidé had nothing to do with the 2019 trade policy often cited in such discussions. He said; “The prolonged closures on the Cameroon border, at Banki and Amchidé, did not arise from the 2019 trade policy at all. They date to 2014, when Boko Haram forced their closure for security reasons, and reopened in 2019, with Fotokol and Gambaru following in 2021, after joint military and stabilisation efforts by Nigeria, Cameroon, Niger and Chad”. The minister said conflating that separate, security-driven history with the 2019 trade-related shutdown misrepresented two distinct issues as a single failure. “Folding this separate, security driven history into one continuous 2019 shutdown misrepresents two distinct issues, trade regulation and counter insurgency, as a single failure,” he said. Tunji-Ojo acknowledged that not every northern crossing is fully unrestricted today, but explained that tighter control in areas experiencing banditry or residual insurgent activity reflects a deliberate security judgement rather than neglect. “Where banditry or residual insurgent activity persists, tighter control is a deliberate security judgement, not neglect, since reopening ahead of the security situation would expose traders and border communities to greater risks,” he said. The minister added that modern border management could not be reduced to a simple choice between total closure and unrestricted movement, stressing that it requires security, documentation, customs compliance and controlled trade facilitation working together. He urged that political competition should not become an avenue to rewrite recent history, challenging Atiku to present a fresh border management proposal rather than merging separate trade, security and infrastructure issues into one narrative. “If he has a new border management proposal, he should set it out and explain how it differs from the current approach, rather than treating separate trade, security and infrastructure issues as one and the same,” he said. The post Nigeria’s borders not closed, Tunji-Ojo tells Atiku appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Tentative de mutinerie au Niger : Le Ministère de la Défense annonce avoir repris le contrôle de la situation
items.description: Un incident militaire a secoué la capitale nigérienne, Niamey, ce samedi 29 août 2026. Selon un communiqué officiel lu à la Télévision nationale, un groupe de soldats « en rupture avec le règlement militaire » a fait usage de ses armes dans plusieurs sites stratégiques de la ville, avant d'être maîtrisé par les forces républicaines. D'après les informations délivrées par le ministre de la Défense nationale, le Général d'armée Salifou Mody, le mouvement a débuté au sein de la caserne de la base 101 de Niamey. Les militaires mutins ont dans un premier temps séquestré certains de leurs camarades avant d'étendre leurs actions à d'autres « sites sensibles » de la capitale, où des tirs ont été signalés. Face à cette situation, le communiqué précise que « la prompte réaction des Forces de défense et de sécurité » (les Forces Armées Nigériennes, FAN) a permis de « circonscrire ce mouvement d'humeur ». Les autorités affirment que le contrôle de ces sites est en train d'être « progressivement » repris, sans toutefois donner plus de détails sur la nature exacte des lieux visés ni sur l'état des forces en présence. Dans ce même message, le Ministère de la Défense su Niger a rassuré la population de Niamey et du pays. Il est demandé aux citoyens de « garder leur calme » et de « vaquer librement à leurs occupations », signalant que la situation est désormais sous contrôle et que la vie normale peut reprendre son cours. items.title: Anta Education Fund beneficiaries rise to 1,519 as Amin Adam supports 200 more students
items.description: Member of Parliament for Karaga and former Finance Minister, Dr Mohammed Amin Adam, has provided financial support to 200 students from various tertiary institutions to enable them to pay their school fees. The latest intervention, which was made in Karaga, forms part of the MP’s ongoing efforts under the Anta Education Fund to ease the financial burden on students and families in the constituency. According to Dr Amin Adam, the latest beneficiaries bring to 1,519 the total number of students who have benefited from the fund since its establishment in 2020. In a Facebook post, Dr Amin Adam said the initiative was established to provide educational support to students in the Pishigu area of the Karaga Constituency and has since expanded its impact across the constituency. He stressed that education remained central to his development agenda, saying, “Education remains our priority; and we will continue to give greater attention to the education of our people.” The Karaga MP said the continued investment in education was necessary to give young people the opportunity to pursue tertiary education despite financial difficulties. “Yesterday in Karaga, we provided support to 200 students from various tertiary educational institutions to pay their fees,” he stated, adding that the intervention had contributed to the growing number of beneficiaries under the Anta Education Fund. The latest initiative further reinforces Dr Amin Adam’s stated commitment to using education as a tool for improving opportunities for young people in the constituency.

items.title: Naqvi visits passport office at Karachi's Awami Markaz, says facility to be expanded
items.description: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on Saturday visited the passport office at Karachi’s Awami Markaz and said the facility would be “expanded for citizens’ convenience”, according to his ministry. A statement by the Ministry of Interior said Naqvi met citizens who were at the centre to seek passports. He asked them about the time it took between the issuance of tokens and their turn at the counter. “Citizens appreciated the passport issuance system and expressed satisfaction,” the ministry said. According to the statement, they also told Naqvi that their work was completed within a few minutes. The citizens also told Naqvi that their work was completed within a few minutes. “No difficulty arose in getting the passport made, nor did they have to wait,” the interior ministry claimed, citing the applicants. In June, officials at Awami Markaz passport office were suspended after a foreign national was issued a Pakistani passport there. Naqvi also visited Jinnah International Airport, where the immigration system malfunctioned as he reviewed the process at the counters, the interior ministry said in a separate statement issued in the morning. The minister contacted relevant officials and directed them to immediately resolve the issue, stressing that arrangements for alternative measures should be ensured in case of such incidents. “The immigration process must not be halted under any circumstances,” Naqvi was quoted as saying. At the airport, the minister also met passengers who were departing for foreign countries and inquired about the immigration process. He ordered strict action against passengers with fake documents, adding that those with incomplete and unverified documents would not be allowed to travel under any circumstances. Naqvi had also visited Karachi in late July, when he met with President Asif Ali Zardari. The month prior, he paid a surprise visit to a mega centre of the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra) in the Safoora Goth area. The interior minister’s remarks earlier this month ignited a fresh debate within political circles after he said the country’s governance system had “collapsed” and proposed to create new provinces. Later, he said the incumbent government would complete its constitutional term. Nisar Ahmed Khuhro of the PPP, which rules Sindh, had demanded Naqvi’s resignation and accused him of undermining the Constitution by “endorsing a hybrid system”.

items.title: OSP dismisses claims of strained relationship with Attorney-General
items.description: The Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP) has rejected perceptions of a strained relationship with the Office of the Attorney-General, insisting that the two institutions maintain a strong working relationship. The Director of Strategy, Research and Communications at the OSP, Samuel Appiah Darko, made the clarification when he called into JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, August 29. According to him, the OSP continues to collaborate effectively with relevant state institutions, particularly the Office of the Attorney-General, in carrying out its anti-corruption mandate. Mr Appiah Darko said that although some members of the public may perceive recent developments as evidence of a clash between the OSP and the Attorney-General, that impression does not reflect the actual relationship between the two offices. “The reason why I have called on the show is to talk about these things. First of all, the issue that the OSP is not collaborating with the AG, I think that it is a wrong perception,” he said. “Is that not obvious from your press conferences?” the host of the show, Samson Lardy Anyenini, asked him. He replied, “I know that people think that there is tension between the AG and the OSP. There could be tension, but you cannot also deny the OSP from also telling Ghanaians about some of the things that it is doing, and it wants to do. For instance, if the OSP needs to respond to some information that has already been put in the public domain that may not be accurate and the OSP clarifies that, that does not mean that the OSP is breeding a fight or tension.” He maintained that the OSP enjoys cordial relations with its stakeholders and remains committed to the institutional cooperation required to investigate and prosecute corruption-related offences effectively. His intervention followed concerns raised during the programme about what appeared to be inadequate collaboration between the OSP and the Attorney-General. Mr Appiah Darko’s remarks sought to assure the public that the two institutions are working together despite differences that may arise in the performance of their respective statutory responsibilities. In recent times, the two institutions have appeared to disagree over their respective roles in Ghana’s fight against corruption, particularly regarding the AKSA bribery allegations and the Abu Trica case. Their public statements have also created the impression of a dispute over which institution deserves credit for the progress made in the two cases.

items.title: Waste crisis: Lagos to deploy 220 more trucks
items.description: Lagos State Government is set to deploy 220 additional trucks to strengthen waste evacuation across the state, Deputy Governor Obafemi Hamzat has said. Hamzat disclosed this on Saturday during the monthly environmental sanitation exercise in Festac, Amuwo-Odofin Local Government Area, explaining that the new trucks would complement the existing Private Sector Participation waste collection system. The planned deployment comes about two months after Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu announced plans to acquire 150 compactor trucks to improve waste management in Lagos. According to the deputy governor, the additional trucks are necessary to cope with the increasing volume of refuse generated as the state’s population continues to grow. “The state government will be bringing in another 220 trucks to make sure that we supplement our PSP. What we need our people to also do is to make sure that they patronise their PSP, not the cart pushers, because they are not organised. You don’t know where the waste is ending up,” Hamzat said. He also urged residents to take responsibility for proper waste disposal, warning that indiscriminate dumping, particularly in drainage channels, could obstruct water flow and contribute to flooding. “A lot of people are coming to Lagos, and therefore they generate waste. So part of what you can see that we are doing is that we are getting many more trucks to actually go and evacuate,” he added. Hamzat stressed that maintaining a clean environment requires cooperation between the government and residents. He encouraged communities to organise regular sanitation exercises and make environmental cleanliness a consistent practice. “We cannot be a people without a healthy environment. It doesn’t matter what we do, a cleaner environment is what makes a city or a state sustainable,” he said. He further urged residents to use approved waste disposal channels and patronise PSP operators rather than relying on unregulated cart pushers. Also speaking during the exercise, the Lagos State Commissioner for the Environment and Water Resources, Tokunbo Wahab, said waste management had improved following the introduction of 24-hour emergency response teams and efforts to address challenges at landfills and dumpsites. Wahab said the state had also stepped up its engagement with PSP operators to improve waste collection, adding that the government had intervened in locations where the Lagos State Waste Management Authority would ordinarily not operate. He said PSP operators had received assurances of government support, while residents were expected to pay for waste collection services under the polluter-pays principle. The commissioner also disclosed that Lagos was gradually moving away from the traditional system of collecting and dumping waste towards a circular model in which discarded materials are recovered and converted into useful resources. According to him, the transition has resulted in the development of material recovery facilities in Badagry and Epe, as well as transfer stations at Soluyi and Olusosun. On cart pushers, Wahab said the government was engaging with them but would not implement measures that could create additional environmental or security challenges. He said investigations had shown that some cart pushers dumped refuse in drainage channels and road medians, worsening flooding and other environmental problems. Wahab also expressed concern over reports linking some cart pushers to criminal activities, including the theft of metals, saying the government would not adopt a policy that could aggravate security challenges in Lagos. items.title: 4e fenêtre éliminatoires Coupe du monde 2027 : duel Sénégal-Angola aujourd’hui à 18 h 30
items.description: Battus jeudi par l’Égypte, à l’occasion de leur première sortie dans cette quatrième fenêtre des éliminatoires de la Coupe du monde 2027, les Lions retrouvent le parquet de Dakar Arena, aujourd’hui. Ils seront opposés à l’Angola à partir de 18 h 30. Un sérieux adversaire pour le Sénégal qui devra impérativement réagir. Après cette défaite d’entrée, les deux derniers matches s’annoncent décisifs pour les Lions qui devront s’imposer pour conserver toutes leurs chances dans la course à la qualification. Avec désormais cinq victoires et deux défaites dans le groupe F, le Sénégal disputera son deuxième match de cette fenêtre, aujourd’hui, à 18 h 30, à Dakar Arena, face aux champions d’Afrique en titre. En effet, les coéquipiers de Brancou Badio qui abordaient ce tournoi sur une série de cinq victoires consécutives, doivent impérativement remporter leurs deux derniers matches contre l’Angola et le Mali après leur revers contre l’Égypte. A lire aussi : Éliminatoires Mondial 2027 de basket : l’Égypte s’impose face au Sénégal Menés de quatre points à l’issue du premier quart-temps, les Égyptiens ont su se ressaisir pour créer la plus grosse surprise parmi les six rencontres disputées jeudi à Dakar (Sénégal) et à Radès (Tunisie). Les Lions, qui ont complètement raté leur match, n’ont pu réussir que 24 tirs sur 70 tentatives. Le meneur de jeu Brancou Badio est sorti de sa zone de confort, manquant ses onze tentatives à 3 points. Il a terminé avec neuf points, son plus faible total depuis le début des Éliminatoires Zone Afrique. Le Sénégal a également été dominé au rebond, 53 à 45, dont un impressionnant total de 23 rebonds offensifs. Face à l’Angola ce samedi, le coach des Lions, DeSagana Diop, devra changer de système et rectifier certaines erreurs. Car l’équipe angolaise, qui fait partie des leaders de ce groupe F, a fait étalage de sa maîtrise défensive, laissant la RDC sans réponse, jeudi à Dakar Arena, lors de la journée d’ouverture des éliminatoires. Les champions d’Afrique en titre ont en effet pris un excellent départ, poussant les Congolais à perdre 22 ballons, un record, avant de s’imposer 100-68. Onze joueurs angolais ont réussi au moins une interception, Cleusio Castro menant la danse avec cinq. Avec 22 interceptions, l’Angola a battu son propre record des Éliminatoires Zone Afrique, établi lors du premier tour de la compétition, lorsqu’il avait terminé avec 21 interceptions lors de sa victoire 90-68 contre l’Ouganda. Absa NDONG

items.title: We’ve asked AG to collaborate on cases but were turned down – OSP
items.description: The Director of Strategy, Research and Communications at the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP), Samuel Appiah Darko, has claimed that the Attorney-General (AG) has declined several requests from the office to collaborate on cases. Mr Appiah Darko said the OSP had, on several occasions, approached the Office of the AG for cooperation but did not receive the requested support. “There are so many issues the OSP has kept quiet and not talked about. Look, there are instances where the OSP has approached the Attorney General’s office and said, let us collaborate in this matter and we have been turned down,” he claimed on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, August 29. His comments followed concerns about an apparent lack of collaboration between the two institutions, which play critical roles in Ghana’s criminal justice system and the fight against corruption. Mr Appiah Darko maintained that although the OSP generally has a good working relationship with the Attorney-General and other stakeholders, there have been instances where its requests for case-specific collaboration were turned down. According to him, several developments occur behind the scenes, but the OSP does not consider it necessary or appropriate to place every institutional interaction in the public domain. “When you are managing a state institution, a very sensitive one, it is not all the information you will come out to the public to talk about,” he noted. Mr Appiah Darko argued that public assessments of the OSP’s performance and institutional relationships should take account of the work and engagements that may not be publicly disclosed.

items.title: Media office rejects ‘northern whisper campaign’ against Peter Obi
items.description: By Henry Umoru The Media Office of the Presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, Peter Obi, has kicked against what it described as false northern whisper campaign against its candidate. According to Peter Obi Media Reach, the circulation of the falsehood regarding Obi’s relationship with northerners during his tenure as governor of Anambra State has persisted despite credible denials from northern leaders in Anambra State, who have explicitly stated that the NDC was, and remains, a vital supporter of theirs both in and out of office. In a statement signed on Saturday, POMR spokesman Idris Zekeri said that Nigeria cannot be rebuilt by weaponising lies that have long divided its people. The statement read, “The Peter Obi Media Office has credible intelligence that some individuals are still conducting malicious whisper campaigns against the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) Presidential Candidate, Peter Obi, in northern rural areas. “The circulation of this falsehood regarding Peter Obi’s relationship with Northerners during his tenure as Governor of Anambra State has persisted despite credible denials from Northern leaders in Anambra State, who have explicitly stated that Obi was, and remains, a vital supporter of theirs both in and out of office. “Despite clear facts, some individuals continue covertly planting these false narratives at Northern gatherings, hoping repeated claims will eventually seem convincing. “We challenge those behind this campaign to provide names, dates, records, and verifiable evidence supporting their allegations. “They should cease hiding behind whispered accusations and political propaganda. “Peter Obi governed Anambra State for all its residents, regardless of ethnicity or religion. His relationship with Nigerians from the North was not based on the falsehoods now being fabricated for political gain. The timing is revealing. “As the 2027 election approaches, those unable to challenge Peter Obi on his competence, integrity, and public service record are resorting to the oldest political weapon—ethnic suspicion and misinformation. “We urge our brothers and sisters in the North to seek facts, not rumours; evidence, not whispers; and policies, not propaganda. “Nigeria cannot be rebuilt by weaponising lies that have long divided its people. Enough of the lies. Let the facts speak for a new Nigeria that is Possible.” The post Media office rejects ‘northern whisper campaign’ against Peter Obi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Rescuers claw through mud as Nepal, China flood missing toll nears 3,000
items.description: Rescuers in Nepal and China were battling Saturday to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region, engulfing entire villages. The latest figures from both countries put the number of missing close to 3,000, with 633 bodies recovered — and reports of some dead possibly swept downstream as far away as India. Rescue worker Kawan Koirala, from the Nepal Scout Disaster Response Team, said they were struggling in thick, leg-sucking mud. “People want their want their family’s body back, either dead or alive, but we cannot find them… you can see the mud,” he told AFP , exhausted after an 18 hour shift. “It is very traumatic for me too. It is my first time seeing these types of things. Everywhere is mud. We faced floods in Nepal before, but not like this.” A man takes pictures in front of damaged buildings after flash floods and a mudslide, in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 29, 2026. — Reuters The US Geological Survey said the disaster on Wednesday on the Tibet-Nepal border was caused by a glacial collapse that created a torrent of debris downstream. Those that made it out say they have lost everything and now face an agonising wait to discover the fate of missing loved ones, and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing. “All the settlements near the river were swept away. There is nothing left,” survivor Buddhi Ram Dangol told AFP . “There is nothing left.” At Bidur’s army base, a key rescue hub in the same district, relatives crowded around lists of rescued people pasted on a wall. Samjhana Thing said she had been waiting three days for news of her missing brother. “We don’t know anything. Hopefully he is in a safe place,” she said. “I have come here looking for my son,” said Kalka Sharda, scanning the list in desperation. “He was a labourer at the hydropower plant, but I can’t find his name, and the authorities are not saying anything.” A person holds an umbrella as he stands in front of damaged buildings after flash floods and a mudslide, in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 29, 2026. — Reuters In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal’s disaster authority listed 933 hydropower workers among the missing, along with 517 foreigners, including trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash. Risk of lake burst near disaster site wanes The threat of a lake formed after the glacier collapse has eased, Chinese authorities said on Saturday, as it appears to have shrunk. Satellite images from Thursday to Saturday morning suggest that water in the lake, which straddles the border between China’s Tibet region and Nepal at the confluence of two rivers, has been slowly flowing out and gradually reducing the reservoir, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the Water Resources Ministry. By Saturday afternoon, parts of the lake bed had become visible, CCTV reported. The ministry said satellite imagery of the lake on the Purepu Tsangpo river showed it covered 99,000 square metres early on Saturday, roughly the size of 14 soccer pitches, having shrunk by 21,000 square metres since Thursday. ‘Enormous’ trauma The trauma of Wednesday’s catastrophe has been “enormous”, and as many as 93,000 people may have been affected, the Red Cross said, with the death toll expected to rise. Emergency teams worked flat out to find survivors as widespread devastation left communities short of food and water. Fears of further flooding have compounded the search for the missing. The deluge of ice and mud caused huge lakes, and one of these formations has become a risk of further floods. While the exact cause of the collapse is unclear, climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of such disasters. Children displaced by flash floods and a mudslide rest inside a relief camp in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 29, 2026. — Reuters In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, Beijing had paused its rescue operation at the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of renewed flooding. On the Nepali side, soldiers were trying desperately to drill through to 100 people trapped in the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project on Saturday. The prime minister’s office said teams had begun “clearing mud and debris” to open the entrance, while a specialised Indian tunnel rescue unit had arrived to help. Nepal reported a death toll of 626 people on Saturday. There are 2,426 people, including hundreds of foreigners, who are out of contact in Nepal. Across the border in Tibet, which is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists, seven people died and 554 remain missing, the state Xinhua news agency said on Saturday. Authorities also said they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet. In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims. ‘All swept away’ On the Nepali side of the border, the military located people trapped in the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where they were working to find a way in to extract the survivors. “Two helicopters have been dispatched, but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel,” army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP . Rescuer load relief material in a helicopter to be transported to the areas affected by flash floods and a mudslide as it drizzles at the Maithali Barrack, an army training center, in Trishuli, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 29, 2026. — Reuters Some 350 workers and residents have been brought to safety from the site, he added, but efforts were ongoing to rescue more than a hundred trapped in the same area. Workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed. Buddha Tamang told AFP he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck. “The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away,” Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours, told AFP . ‘Pilgrimage route’ Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among those missing on the border, as many were on a pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash. Sivaranjani Muthunathan was travelling by bus with 56 others towards the Chinese border when they became stuck in what they thought was a traffic jam. “Then there was fog, smoke, something that seemed to suddenly engulf us,” Muthunathan, 46, told AFP on Friday, showing a phone video she recorded of a torrent surging towards her. A man walks past a damaged house after the flash floods and mudslide, at Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 29, 2026. — Reuters Around them, vehicles were swept away or buried under mud. “One by one, we also climbed out through the driver’s side,” then scrambled up a hill, she said.

items.title: OSP must be judged by its mandate, not who occupies the office – Baffour Awuah
items.description: The Member of Parliament for Manhyia South, Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah, has called on Ghanaians to avoid defining the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP) by the personality of the individual occupying the position. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, August 29, the MP argued that public discussions about the OSP should focus on the institution, its legal mandate and its performance rather than the officeholder. “We should avoid personalising the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP). I listened to the press conference, and I was sad that you came and said that all that is happening is because of hatred for the occupant of the office. Very respectfully was below the belt,” he said. “Why would you want to believe or make it seem that it is a personal matter against the occupant of the office?, While you take that position, it becomes very difficult for cooperation,” he added. His comments followed the OSP’s recent press conference, during which the anti-corruption body declared its “rebirth” and reaffirmed its commitment to fighting corruption. The discussion also examined emerging concerns, including what appears to be inadequate collaboration between the OSP and the Office of the Attorney-General. Mr Awuah maintained that personalising the OSP could weaken public confidence in the institution and distract attention from broader questions about its effectiveness and relationship with other state agencies. He called for the OSP to be treated as an enduring state institution whose credibility and operations should not depend solely on the person serving as Special Prosecutor.

items.title: OSP says intervention has reduced corruption in GRA Customs vehicle auctions
items.description: The Director of Strategy, Research and Communications at the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP), Samuel Appiah Darko, says the office’s intervention has helped reduce corruption within the Customs Division of the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA). Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, August 29, Mr Appiah Darko said the OSP was undertaking significant anti-corruption work that was not always publicised. He cited the sanitisation of vehicle auction processes within the Customs Division as one of the OSP’s notable interventions. Mr Appiah Darko said the intervention had helped sanitise the auction system and minimise opportunities for corruption within the division. “If you go to the Customs Division, in the past you would hear a lot of wrong about auction vehicles, now it is reduced. It is the work of the OSP. We had to change the benchmark value that was given to Customs Officials, the opportunity to be able to engage in corruption and all that; the OSP is the one that brought all these things to an end through the work we did in the Labianca case and all that,” he said. He argued that the impact of the OSP should not be assessed solely by the cases or investigations it announces publicly, as some of its work involves behind-the-scenes interventions aimed at preventing corruption. He, therefore, rejected claims that the OSP was doing little to combat corruption, insisting that the office continued to deliver results across various public institutions.

items.title: Igbos built Nollywood but Yorubas have become dominant — Francis Duru
items.description: Veteran Nollywood actor Francis Duru has sparked debate with his views on the changing ethnic influence within Nigeria’s film industry, arguing that the Yoruba community has become more dominant because of its ability to organise and promote its own. In a recent interview on Gbam, aired on the Yan Content Factory YouTube channel on Friday, Duru acknowledged the contributions of Yoruba pioneers such as Herbert Ogunde to Nigerian theatre and performance arts in the 1950s. However, he argued that the modern Nollywood home-video industry was largely driven by Igbo entrepreneurs during the 1990s and early 2000s. According to the actor, Igbo traders played a major role in developing the home-video market that eventually evolved into the Nollywood industry known globally today. Duru argued that the Yoruba community was more effective at pooling resources, creating opportunities for its members and protecting its cultural interests. “The Yorubas epitomise the saying, ‘Charity begins at home.’ We need to learn from them. If you don’t protect and project your own, who will do it?” he said. He also cited streaming platforms such as Netflix as evidence of what he described as the decline in the visibility of Igbo stories within Nollywood. “We [Igbos] created Nollywood, but if you go to Netflix today, you hardly see one movie that speaks of Igbo heritage. But the Yorubas, on the other hand, created opportunities for themselves and utilised them,” Duru stated. The actor blamed what he described as an individualistic mindset among some Igbos for the loss of influence. “Igbos failed to learn because of their individualistic mentality. You think you are the big man, so you are self-centred. But you forget that a time will come when you need to be expansive,” he said. Duru further expressed concern that Igbo history and culture are increasingly being portrayed by filmmakers from outside the community. “We have great writers who are now writing for the Yorubas. You even see the Yorubas crossing over to write Igbo stories like Ahamefuna and making a mess of who we are,” he said. Despite his criticism, Duru said his comments should not be interpreted as an attack on Yoruba filmmakers. Instead, he urged Igbos to learn from how the Yoruba community has promoted its own people and culture. “Don’t get angry with them. These are people who saw their own and protected their own. What happened to you?” he asked. He also questioned why more films had not been made about prominent Igbo figures and historical personalities. “Igbos have many great men in Nigeria. When was the last time you saw the epic of one of these great men?” Duru asked. His comments have since generated discussions around ethnicity, cultural ownership, collective investment and representation in Nigeria’s entertainment industry. items.title: Trust, judgment and value: The 3 questions every organisation must answer about AI
items.description: Over the past year, I have participated in numerous conversations with boards, executives, and business leaders about artificial intelligence. While these discussions often begin with excitement about the technology’s potential, they almost always converge on a few underlying concerns. The questions are not usually about whether AI is powerful. Most leaders already recognise that it is. Instead, the conversation usually comes down to three fundamental questions: Can we trust it? Is it creating value? Who remains accountable? These questions may appear straightforward, but they will often determine whether AI becomes a source of lasting business value or simply another technology experiment. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in business processes and decision-making, the challenge for leaders is no longer just adopting the technology. It is ensuring that it is used responsibly, effectively, and with appropriate oversight. Can We Trust It? Trust has always been a cornerstone of business success. Investors rely on accurate information to make decisions. Customers trust organisations with their data. Employees trust leadership to act responsibly. Without trust, confidence erodes and performance suffers. AI introduces new questions into that equation. Unlike traditional systems that operate according to predefined rules, AI models often generate outputs based on patterns in data. While this can produce remarkable results, it can also make outcomes more difficult to explain and understand. As organisations adopt AI, leaders must ask important questions: How reliable is the data being used? How are AI outputs being validated? What controls exist to identify errors or bias? Who oversees ongoing performance? These are not purely technology concerns. They are governance concerns. Regulators across the world are increasingly paying attention to how AI is governed, and Africa is unlikely to be an exception. In Ghana, organisations are already subject to requirements around data privacy, cybersecurity, and responsible handling of information. While AI-specific regulation is still evolving, the direction of travel is clear. Boards and management teams will increasingly be expected to understand how AI systems operate, what data they rely on, and how associated risks are managed. The organisations building these governance foundations today will be better prepared for tomorrow’s regulatory expectations. The reality is that trust cannot be assumed simply because a system is sophisticated. It must be earned through transparency, oversight and accountability. Organisations that establish clear governance around AI will be better positioned to build confidence among customers, employees, investors, and regulators. In many ways, trust will become a key differentiator in the AI era. Technology may be widely accessible, but confidence in how it is deployed will not be. Is It Creating Value? The second question is equally important. Today, many organisations are investing heavily in AI initiatives. New tools are being deployed, pilot projects are being launched, and employees are being encouraged to integrate AI into their daily work. Yet one question continues to surface in boardrooms: Where is the measurable value? The assumption that AI adoption automatically leads to productivity gains can be misleading. Technology alone rarely transforms an organisation. Sustainable value typically requires changes to processes, skills, ways of working, and performance measurement. Simply providing employees with AI tools does not guarantee better outcomes. In fact, some organisations are experiencing what might be described as an AI productivity paradox. Work is being completed faster. More content is being produced. Information is easier to access. Yet improvements in business performance are often harder to demonstrate. This should not be surprising. Every major technological shift has required organisations to rethink how work is done before meaningful benefits can be realised. The most successful organisations are focusing less on adoption metrics and more on business outcomes. Rather than asking how many employees are using AI, they are asking: Has decision-making improved? Have risks been reduced? Has customer experience improved? Have costs been lowered? Is productivity genuinely increasing? Ultimately, the objective is not to deploy AI for its own sake. The objective is to create value. Leaders who remain focused on outcomes rather than hype will be far more likely to realise meaningful returns from their investments. Who Remains Accountable? The third question may be the most important. As AI becomes more capable, there is a growing temptation to view technology as a substitute for human judgment. That would be a mistake. AI can analyse information at extraordinary speed. It can identify patterns, generate insights, and support complex decision-making. However, it cannot assume responsibility for the consequences of those decisions. Accountability remains a human responsibility. Business decisions are rarely based on data alone. They require context, experience, professional scepticism, ethical considerations, and an understanding of stakeholder expectations. A board evaluating a strategic investment must consider factors that extend beyond projections and forecasts. A management team responding to a crisis must weigh commercial, reputational, and social implications. An auditor assessing risk must apply judgment in situations where there may be no clear answer. These responsibilities cannot be delegated to algorithms. In fact, as AI becomes more prevalent, human judgment may become more valuable. The ability to challenge assumptions, interpret complex situations, and make balanced decisions will remain essential. The future of work is unlikely to be defined by humans competing against AI. Rather, it will be shaped by organisations that successfully combine technological capability with human insight. The best outcomes will come not from AI alone, but from people who know how to use it wisely. Looking Ahead AI represents one of the most significant technological developments of our time. Its potential to improve efficiency, enhance decision-making, and drive innovation is undeniable. However, organisations should resist the temptation to view AI solely through a technology lens. The more important questions are ultimately about leadership, governance, and accountability. Can we trust it? Is it creating value? Who remains accountable? The organisations that answer these questions effectively will be best positioned to realise the benefits of AI while managing its risks. Technology will continue to evolve. The principles of trust, value, and sound judgment will not. In the age of AI, those principles may matter more than ever.
